header: MANS-HIS-203 · Microbiology — Hypersensitivity classification, authored from the His Continuous Berlin Book 2026 (Microbiology L1 revision, p.46), printed keys. Three questions test the new Gell-Coombs classification concept minted for this batch; one tests an existing live basophil/mast-cell concept.

defaults.subject: imm
defaults.source_citation: His Continuous Berlin Book 2026, Microbiology L1 revision, p.46

questions.title: Pollen and hypersensitivity type
questions.question: Pollen would most likely evoke which type of hypersensitivity?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Type II is antibody bound directly to a fixed antigen on a cell or tissue surface, destroying that cell; pollen allergy has no fixed cellular target of that kind.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Type III is antibody bound to soluble circulating antigen forming immune complexes that deposit in tissue; that is not the mechanism behind pollen allergy either.
explanations.C: Correct. Pollen most likely evokes a type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction. Pollen-specific IgE sits bound to mast cells and basophils, and pollen cross-linking that surface IgE triggers degranulation within minutes. That immediate histamine release is what produces the symptoms of allergic rhinitis or asthma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Type IV is T-cell-mediated and delayed, developing over 24-72 hours with no antibody involved; pollen allergy is instead an immediate, antibody (IgE)-mediated reaction.

questions.learning_objective: Classify pollen allergy as a type I (IgE-mediated immediate) hypersensitivity reaction.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.46

questions.title: Antibody class that cross-links mast cells
questions.question: Which of the following binds to mast cells and cross-links, resulting in degranulation and release of histamine?

explanations.A: Incorrect. IgM is the first antibody made in a primary immune response and fixes complement efficiently; it does not bind mast-cell surface receptors the way IgE does.
explanations.B: Incorrect. IgG mediates type II and III hypersensitivity mechanisms and crosses the placenta, but it is not the antibody class that sits bound to resting mast cells awaiting antigen.
explanations.C: Incorrect. IgD is mainly a B-cell surface receptor involved in B-cell activation, not an antibody that arms mast cells for degranulation.
explanations.D: Correct. IgE is the antibody class that binds high-affinity receptors on the surface of mast cells and basophils. When antigen cross-links two adjacent surface-bound IgE molecules, the cell degranulates within minutes, releasing histamine and other mediators — the mechanism behind type I hypersensitivity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify IgE as the antibody class that binds mast cells and, on antigen cross-linking, triggers degranulation and histamine release.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.46

questions.title: Mechanism of type I hypersensitivity
questions.question: The mechanism of action of type I hypersensitivity involves:

options.A: Production of IgE in response to certain antigens
options.B: Production of IgG in response to certain antigens
options.C: Production of IgM in response to certain antigens
options.D: Production of IgA in response to certain antigens

explanations.A: Correct. Type I hypersensitivity begins with IgE production against a specific antigen (an allergen). That IgE binds mast cells and basophils, and re-exposure to the same antigen cross-links the surface-bound IgE, triggering immediate degranulation and the type I reaction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. IgG production is the antibody mechanism behind type II (cytotoxic) and type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity, not type I.
explanations.C: Incorrect. IgM is the antibody typically made early in a primary response and, like IgG, can participate in type II mechanisms via complement fixation; it is not the antibody class defining type I.
explanations.D: Incorrect. IgA is the antibody of mucosal secretions and is not the mechanism that defines type I hypersensitivity.

questions.learning_objective: State that IgE production against a specific antigen is the mechanism that defines type I hypersensitivity.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.46

questions.title: Penicillin and pollen hypersensitivity share a mechanism
questions.question: Hypersensitivity to drugs like penicillin and hypersensitivity to pollen grains are both:

explanations.A: Incorrect. IgM is not the antibody class responsible for either penicillin's immediate allergic reactions or pollen allergy.
explanations.B: Correct. Penicillin hypersensitivity and pollen hypersensitivity are both mediated by IgE antibody, even though the two triggers — a drug and a plant allergen — are completely different substances. The Gell and Coombs classification sorts a reaction by its mechanism, not by what triggered it, and both of these are type I, IgE-mediated reactions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. IgG mediates other hypersensitivity mechanisms (type II, type III), not the immediate, mast-cell-degranulating mechanism shared by penicillin and pollen allergy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. IgA is the secretory antibody of mucosal surfaces, not the mediator of either penicillin's or pollen's immediate allergic reactions.
explanations.E: Incorrect. IgD functions mainly as a B-cell surface receptor, not as the effector antibody in either of these two reactions.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that penicillin and pollen hypersensitivity share the same IgE-mediated type I mechanism despite having different triggers, illustrating that hypersensitivity type is read from mechanism, not trigger.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.46
